Forgot Password First, we go to the Forgot Password function. 2. Target email We enter the email address we want to target. 3. Valid OTP baseline Before starting the attack, we first use the real OTP code to understand how the server behaves when it receives a valid code. This gives us a baseline for comparison. 4. Burp interception Now we start intercepting the traffic using Burp Suite. Here, we can see the request and response. 5. Normal flow We save the response for later comparison. As we can see, the process works normally and the application takes us to the password-changing function. 6. Password change intercept Next, we try to change the password while intercepting the requests and responses. 7. Password requirements check The first request is not important for the bypass. It is only used to check whether the password meets the application's requirements. 8. Password change request After this request, we get the actual password-changing request. 9. Successful HTTP 200 From the normal flow, we can see that the successful requests return HTTP 200 OK. 10. Wrong OTP attempt Now we try using a wrong OTP code. 11. Incorrect code entered The previous flow used the real OTP. This time, we intentionally enter an incorrect code. 12. Invalid OTP response If we submit the wrong code normally, the application tells us that the OTP is invalid. We use Burp Suite to intercept the response and see how the server responds. Status Code Difference The server returns: HTTP/2 400 Bad Request From the legitimate flow, we know that a successful request returns: HTTP/2 200 OK This gives us an interesting difference between the valid and invalid flows. First Bypass — OTP Validation We intercept the response and modify the status code from 400 Bad Request to 200 OK . After forwarding the modified response, the application accepts the response and takes us to the password-changing page. Second OTP Check However, when we try to complete the password change, the application performs another OTP validation. The request still returns 400, meaning that the OTP is being verified again during the password-changing stage. Second Bypass — Password Change We then perform the same response manipulation on the next validation response and change the status code to 200 OK . After this, the application accepts the modified responses and completes the password-reset process. Root Cause The main issue is response manipulation via HTTP status codes . The client is using the server's response status to determine whether the OTP verification was successful. Since the response can be intercepted and modified before the client processes it, this should not be trusted as a security boundary. Impact Full account takeover on any user whose email is known. An attacker can reset the victim's password without ever possessing a valid OTP — only a MITM position (Burp Suite proxy) is required. Remediation Never rely on HTTP status codes alone for security decisions on the client side. Validate OTP server-side and bind the reset session to a server-issued token only issued after successful verification. Use cryptographically signed response bodies; reject tampered responses. Implement certificate pinning or HSTS where applicable to raise the bar for interception (defense in depth, not a sole fix).

Writeups/index.title: Writeups
Writeups/index.content: Writeups Real bug bounty findings, step by step. Each writeup covers the recon that surfaced the target, the vulnerability, exploitation, and what made the report land. What Goes Here Disclosed or redacted bounty reports CTF and lab walkthroughs with transferable techniques Chain breakdowns showing how medium findings became critical payouts Writeups Password Reset OTP Bypass via Response Manipulation Using HTTP Status Codes — Critical ATO by rewriting HTTP 400 to 200 on OTP validation responses in Burp Suite. Writeup Template When adding a new writeup, include: Target & scope — program, asset, tech stack Recon — how you found the entry point Vulnerability — root cause and affected component Exploitation — PoC with requests/screenshots Impact — what an attacker could actually do Takeaways — what to look for on similar targets See also: Reporting and Chains .

index.title: The Bug Bounty Playbook
index.content: A living collection of TTPs, methodology, and tradecraft for bug bounty hunting. Opinionated and incomplete. Some pages are polished, some are rough notes jotted down between targets. A finished playbook would mean I stopped learning, so don't hold your breath. Who this is for Hunters who already know the basics. If you need someone to explain what Burp Suite does, start with PortSwigger's Web Security Academy and come back when you've done the practitioner-level labs. If you're past that and want to find bugs that actually pay, chain findings into crits, and navigate the business side of bounty hunting, you're in the right place. Sections Methodology Zero to payout Recon Discovery, enumeration, target mapping Attack Surface Web, API, mobile, cloud, CI/CD Chains Multi-vuln escalation patterns Tooling Configs, scripts, and automation Reporting Reports that get paid, not triaged as informational Programs Platform strategy, program selection, the meta-game Business of Bounties The stuff nobody talks about Writeups Real findings, exploitation steps, and lessons learned Open the graph view to see how everything connects. Every technique links to the recon that surfaces it, the chains that escalate it, and the reporting patterns that get it paid. Philosophy PoC or GTFO. Every technique page should give you something you can run right now. Theory belongs in a textbook. Chain thinking. A single medium is fine. Two mediums chained into a critical is a career. Every time you find something, ask what it lets you reach next. The report is the product. You don't get paid for finding bugs. You get paid for convincing triage that what you found matters. Excellent findings get closed as informational when the report is two sentences and a screenshot. Tags Pages are tagged by difficulty, severity potential, and attack surface. Contributions and feedback welcome. About I'm Alae Eddine, a 17-year-old penetration tester and bug bounty hunter from Morocco. I started my cybersecurity journey in 2024, focusing on penetration testing, web application security, bug bounty, and red teaming. I spend most of my time hunting for vulnerabilities, practicing on platforms like Hack The Box and TryHackMe, and improving my offensive security skills through hands-on research. This playbook is based on the practical methodology I've developed through real-world research, labs, and experience. Find me on X/Twitter .
